sections.html: Occurs in pebbly beds in swift currents at the base of hills. Found among rocks and boulders on the bottom of fast flowing upland streams.

In their natural habitat their diet consists of aquatic insects and larvae. In an aquarium set-up they like worm foods such as frozen bloodworm and whiteworm. They feed very much like the Tatia species from South America, feeding frantically on the move, twisting and turning to take the food.
Best kept with larger Danios such as the Giant Danio (Danio aequipinnatus), barbs and rasboras: medium-sized fish that like water movement in the aquarium.
Females have a pair of unbranched ovaries and are smaller than the males who have branched testes.

Description: Differs from A. mucronatum, A. murraystuarti, A. platycephalus, A. foratum and A. variegatum in having a relatively short body with 34-36 (versus 38-40) vertebrae, and a caudal fin with upper and lower lobes of distinctly different shapes (versus truncate caudal fin in A. murraystuarti and with both lobes similar in shape in other Indochinese species). Pectoral spine smooth.

Etymology: The specific name mangois is a Latinisation of Manggoi, the local Gangetic name for this catfish.

IUCN Red List: Although some anthropogenic threats to this species have been documented (Prasad et al. 1997), these are deemed to be speculative and not based on hard evidence. Given that this species is relatively common and abundant throughout the sub-Himalayan region (in the Ganges and Brahmaputra river drainages), Amblyceps mangois is assessed as Least Concern here, but needs updating (IUCN 2010).
